analysis.title: The Flow Show: A Tail of Two Cities
key_insights: Hartnett frames the market as best of times and worst of times: financial conditions are tightening and crushing equity breadth (400 S&P 500 stocks below the 50-day average, 300 below the 200-day) while the market trades 'long artificial intelligence' (NDX) and 'short artificial irrelevance' (equal-weight S&P). Mag7, AI and biotech are described as unaffected by higher rates, and the 1999 analog is called intact.

BofA's stance is risk-off until the US dollar peaks. The dollar is rising on credit event risk, with stress shown in the Australian dollar, French bonds, risk parity (RPAR), bond insurers (AGO) and tech CDS (ORCL), which BofA reads as deleveraging price action.

BofA sees the threat of policy panic (open-ended Treasury buybacks, yield curve control) as limiting downside, because policymakers cannot let yields hit the AI capex boom and stocks into the midterms. The exception is if small/mid-caps (MDY below $666, IJR below $135) follow banks into a breakdown. 'Peak growth optimism' is negative for tech.

Bull case: 'it's the railroads this time'. Peak concentration was about 40% for internet, Japan, Nifty Fifty and the roaring 20s bubbles, but 63% for railroads in 1881. AI capex of 3.5-4% of GDP compares with a 5% railroad peak, and semiconductor prices are rising, whereas freight rates deflated at the railroad top.

Bear case in the railroad analogy: railroad booms were backstopped by falling Treasury yields, which is not the case today. Railroad tops in 1873, 1881, 1973 and 1981 coincided with credit events, sharp liquidity declines and capital outflows tied to geopolitical events.

The BofA Bull & Bear Indicator fell to 8.8 from 9.3, which is a Sell signal. The drivers were wider spreads in risky bonds, HY bond outflows, and deteriorating global index breadth (net 27% of global equity indices below both the 50-day and 200-day averages, worst since March 2026). The 'old' indicator is at 6.2.

On bonds, BofA says a credit event or recession is needed for a 100-200bp fall in yields. Asset allocators are very long stocks and very short bonds, so BofA says 'buy humiliation' and start adding bonds. Long-run Treasury returns are the worst in 100 years, which BofA treats as an entry point.

US IG tech bond prices (CITE) are down 9% over the past year and yields rose from 4.5% to 6.2%. BofA says that because AI is backstopped by the US government, hyperscaler long bond yields (Oracle 8.4%, Meta 7.5%, Google 6.9%) may soon attract buyers.
Weekly flows: $18.8bn to bonds, $15.8bn to stocks, $0.9bn to crypto, $0.7bn to gold, and $118.0bn out of cash on quarter-end. Investors are starting to nibble at bonds and bond-sensitive sectors.

Notable flow records: long-term bonds took $7.4bn (largest since May 2025) and municipal bonds took $4.2bn (largest ever, data since 2004). Europe equities took $1.3bn (largest since Feb 2026), China equities $3.7bn (largest in 9 weeks), tech $3.3bn (largest in 5 weeks) and utilities $1.0bn (largest since Dec 2025).

BofA private clients hold $4.6tn AUM: 66.3% stocks (record high), 17.1% bonds and 9.4% cash (record low). Mag7 is 16% of AUM, Treasuries 4% and gold 0.3%. They made the largest weekly purchases of 2-10 year Treasury notes in 2 months and, in ETFs over four weeks, bought bank loans, munis and TIPS while selling utilities, tech and financials.
Q3 winners were bitcoin (+43%), oil (+42%), software (+18%) and Mag7 (+11%). Losers were zero-coupon bonds (-15%), semis (-11%), industrials (-10%) and Korea (-8%).
YTD scores: oil +61.8%, global stocks +12.1%, US stocks +12.0%, US dollar +3.8%, cash +2.7%, HY bonds -0.3%, IG -3.2%, bitcoin -3.4%, gold -3.8%, government bonds -4.1%.

Fixed income flows: IG inflows for 2 weeks ($3.5bn), HY outflows resumed ($1.4bn), EM debt inflows for 9 weeks ($2.3bn), Treasury inflows for 14 weeks ($10.8bn). US equities saw outflows for 2 weeks ($2.7bn), while Japan, Europe and EM took inflows.

BofA's contrarian indicators: the FMS cash indicator reads 3.9% (Sell, at or below 4.0%), the Global Breadth Rule reads -27.3% (Neutral), and the Global Flow Trading Rule reads 0.0% (Neutral). The Global EPS Growth Model reads 35% with EPS growth rising.

Utilities took $1.0bn of inflows, the largest since December 2025, while BofA private clients sold utilities ETFs over four weeks.
A breakdown below MDY $666 and IJR $135 would remove the policy-backstop limit on downside.

tension_points.bull_case: AI hyperscaler capex of 3.5-4% of GDP in 2027 is still below the roughly 5% railroad peak, and semiconductor prices are soaring rather than deflating as freight rates did.
tension_points.bear_case: Railroad booms were backstopped by falling Treasury yields, which is not the case today, and railroad tops coincided with credit events, liquidity declines and capital outflows.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A credit or liquidity event, or small/mid-caps breaking down (MDY below $666, IJR below $135), would weaken the bull case.

tension_points.bull_case: Policy panic (open-ended Treasury buybacks, yield curve control) limits downside because policymakers cannot let yields hit the AI capex boom and stocks into the midterms.
tension_points.bear_case: Credit event risk is lifting the dollar, with deleveraging in AUD, French bonds, risk parity, bond insurers and tech CDS.
tension_points.what_invalidates: MDY below $666 and IJR below $135 as small/mid-caps follow banks into a breakdown.
